topic: understanding the concept of geometric series and their sum formula

easy.text: A geometric series is the sum of terms in a geometric sequence, where each term is found by:

options.text: Multiplying the previous term by a constant ratio
options.feedback: Correct -- a geometric sequence (and thus the series formed by summing it) uses a fixed multiplicative ratio between consecutive terms.

options.text: Adding a constant value to the previous term
options.feedback: That describes an ARITHMETIC sequence/series, not a geometric one, which specifically uses MULTIPLICATION by a constant ratio, not addition.

options.text: Squaring the previous term each time
options.feedback: Squaring isn't the defining operation for a geometric sequence -- it specifically uses multiplication by a FIXED constant ratio, not squaring.

options.text: There is no consistent pattern between terms
options.feedback: A geometric sequence DOES have a very definite, consistent pattern -- a fixed multiplicative ratio between consecutive terms.

medium.text: Find the sum of the first 4 terms of the geometric series: 2+6+18+54... (using the formula Sn=a(1-r^n)/(1-r), where a=first term, r=common ratio, n=number of terms)

options.feedback: This is close to 3⁴ but doesn't correctly apply the full sum formula for this geometric series.

hard.text: An INFINITE geometric series (with infinitely many terms) can have a finite sum ONLY if the absolute value of the common ratio (|r|) is less than 1, using the formula S=a/(1-r). Why does this specific condition (|r|<1) matter for whether an infinite sum can actually converge to a finite value?

options.text: When |r|<1, each successive term becomes progressively smaller in magnitude, causing the total sum to approach (converge toward) a specific finite value as more terms are added, whereas if |r|≥1, terms would stay the same size or grow, causing the sum to grow without bound (diverge) rather than converging
options.feedback: Correct -- this specific mathematical condition (|r|<1) is precisely what determines whether an infinite geometric series will converge to a finite, well-defined sum, or instead diverge toward infinity (or oscillate without settling to a specific value).

options.text: An infinite series can actually always be summed to a finite value, regardless of the common ratio's magnitude
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- an infinite geometric series can ONLY be summed to a finite value specifically when |r|<1; otherwise, the sum diverges (grows without bound or doesn't settle to a specific value).

options.text: The magnitude of the common ratio has no actual connection to whether an infinite series converges or diverges
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- the magnitude of the common ratio is actually THE central, determining factor for whether an infinite geometric series converges (to a finite sum) or diverges.

options.text: When |r|<1, the terms actually get progressively LARGER, which is why the sum can be finite
options.feedback: This is backwards -- when |r|<1, terms get progressively SMALLER (not larger), which is precisely why the total sum can approach and converge to a finite value.
